item.research_question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via in-situ alloy formation using laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence defect formation, microstructure, and phase composition?
item.material_system: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 (refractory metal high entropy alloy) fabricated from a heterogeneous mixture of elemental W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V powders.
item.processing_route: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm) on a Mo substrate in Argon atmosphere (<25 ppm O2). Two parameter sets were used: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch, 125 J/mm³) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch, 889 J/mm³). Vanadium powder content was increased by a factor of 1.5 to compensate for evaporation.
item.test_conditions: Samples (6 × 6 × 6 mm³) were analyzed via optical microscopy, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and microhardness testing. Microhardness was measured as HV0.1. Cooling rates are estimated at 10⁶ K/s.
key_findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.
A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD and TEM, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.
Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.
Parameter set B (higher volumetric energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved tungsten particles compared to set A.
Parameter set A exhibited smaller cracks than set B, which showed wider cracks due to higher internal stress.
Microhardness of the coarser structure (Set A) was 561 ± 17 HV0.1, while the finer cellular structure (Set B) was 614 ± 21 HV0.1.
Elemental segregation was observed: V concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly in intradendritic areas.
Solidification mode shifted from dendritic (Set A) to cellular (Set B) based on growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G) conditions.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the formation of undissolved W particles to the high melting point of tungsten, which requires high volumetric energy input and slow scan speeds to dissolve. Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the PBF-LB/M process combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and brittle grain boundaries (likely due to O and N impurities). The microstructure (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) to temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites, while lower R and higher G favor cellular structures.
item.limitations: Samples contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; completely defect-free samples were not produced. The study notes that the alloy has limited room temperature ductility and fracture toughness.
item.future_work: The authors suggest using a high-temperature (>600 °C) build-platform heating device and/or high-purity powder with low O and N content to achieve crack-free processing. They also propose verifying if more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility can be processed without high-temperature heating.
quotes: The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%.
The average grain size determined by the linear intercept method is 16.3 µm. This is more than a factor of four smaller than the 80 µm reported by Senkov et al. for vacuum arc molten samples.

Cracking of the already solidified material due to internal stress induced by the PBF-LB/M process and an insufficient ductility of the material at lower temperatures is assumed to be the cause for the cracks.
